summary: Chinese word order is fixed, and it carries much of the grammar: subject – (time) – (place) – verb – object. The place, with 在, comes before the verb: 我在家吃饭 ‘I eat at home’ — never after it as in English or German. The small words that modify the verb — 不 and 没 (S08), 都, 也 and 只 (S09) — stand right before it (or before 在 + place): 我们都不喝啤酒 ‘none of us drinks beer’. A topic can open the sentence: 早饭我吃面包 or 我早饭吃面包 ‘for breakfast I have bread’. Questions keep the same order (S09, S10).

items: 不 / 都 / 也 / 只

items.title: Chinese: the verb after time and place

blocks.title: The place does not follow the verb
blocks.text: ‘I eat at home’ is 我在家吃饭 — *我吃饭在家 copies English and is wrong.

blocks.title: Adverbs stick to the verb
blocks.text: 都 ‘all’, 也 ‘also’, 只 ‘only’, 不 and 没 stand right before the verb, or before 在 + place: 我们都在家吃饭 ‘we all eat at home’, 他不在家吃饭 ‘he doesn’t eat at home’.

blocks.title: Topic first
blocks.text: Something already in the conversation can open the sentence: 早饭我吃面包 / 我早饭吃面包 ‘breakfast — I have bread’. The rest keeps its order.

blocks.title: Like Turkish — almost
blocks.text: Turkish also puts time and place before the verb (Ben evde yemek yerim ‘I eat at home’); Chinese differs in putting the object after the verb: 我在家吃饭.

askYourself: Who? → first (a topic or a time word may come before it).
When? → a time word before the verb, before or after the subject (S14).
Where? → 在 + place before the verb.
Is there 不, 没, 都, 也 or 只? → right before the verb (or before 在 + place).
What? → the object after the verb.
steps: adverb (不 / 都 / 也 / 只)

traps: *我吃饭在家 → 我在家吃饭.
*我们喝都茶 → 我们都喝茶.
German V2 does not apply: *今天吃我面包 → 今天我吃面包.

quiz.why: 都 after the subject, before the verb.

seeAlso.note: German keeps the verb in second place and can front the object (Den Tee trinke ich) because the accusative shows the role; Chinese keeps subject – (time) – (place) – verb – object.
Arabic often starts with the verb (يَشْرَبُ الْوَلَدُ الشَّايَ ‘the boy drinks the tea’) and its case endings allow other orders; a Chinese sentence never starts with the verb in a statement.
Hebrew is subject – verb – object like Chinese, but the place usually follows the verb (אֲנִי אוֹכֵל בַּבַּיִת); Chinese puts it before: 我在家吃饭.
